title: Hungarian Goulash for the Crew
seoTitle: Hungarian Goulash for the Crew | Firefighter Meal
shortDescription: Paprika beef stew with caraway and potatoes for ten
subtitle: Paprika beef stew with caraway and potatoes for ten
description: Beef chuck simmers with onions, potatoes, and a heavy hand of sweet paprika until the broth turns rust-red and meat breaks down tender. Serve in deep bowls with sour cream and rye bread.

steps.title: Gather ingredients and equipment
steps.instruction: Line up every ingredient for Hungarian Goulash for the Crew in the order you will cook — measure spices into ramekins, trim proteins on a dedicated board, and set tongs, thermometers, and hotel pans within arm's reach before any heat goes on.

steps.title: Preheat ovens and surfaces
steps.instruction: Preheat ovens, griddles, or grills to recipe temp before the crew arrives — cold equipment extends cook time and dries out batch beef. Confirm burners ignite evenly and sheet pans are greased or lined.

steps.title: Brown the beef
steps.instruction: Season chuck cubes and brown in batches in a Dutch oven over high heat until deeply colored. Set aside. Bake until the center reaches a safe internal temp (145°F for medium beef, 160°F for ground) and edges look set — use a thermometer at the thickest point. Plan about 15 minutes for this step at crew scale.

steps.title: Cook onions and spices
steps.instruction: Reduce heat, add onions, and cook 8 minutes. Stir in paprika, caraway, garlic, and tomato paste, cooking 2 minutes until fragrant.

steps.title: Simmer the stew
steps.instruction: Return beef, add broth and bell pepper. Cover and simmer 1.5 hours until beef starts to tenderize. Maintain a steady simmer — bubbles should break the surface without a rolling boil that shreds delicate proteins. Work in batches if the pan or grill crowding steams food instead of browning — rookies should watch for pale surfaces and adjust heat early. Target 145°F for steaks, 160°F for ground at the thickest point before moving to the next batch.

steps.title: Add potatoes
steps.instruction: Stir in potatoes and simmer uncovered 30–40 minutes until beef and potatoes are fork-tender and broth thickens slightly. Maintain a steady simmer — bubbles should break the surface without a rolling boil that shreds delicate proteins. Work in batches if the pan or grill crowding steams food instead of browning — rookies should watch for pale surfaces and adjust heat early. Target 145°F for steaks, 160°F for ground at the thickest point before moving to the next batch.

steps.title: Verify safe internal temps
steps.instruction: Spot-check the thickest pieces with an instant-read thermometer — target 145°F for medium beef, 160°F for ground. If any piece reads low, return it to heat immediately rather than holding under temp on the line.

steps.title: Hold for call interruptions
steps.instruction: If tones drop mid-service, cover finished food and hold at 140°F in a warm cabinet or 200°F oven — never leave proteins below 140°F for more than 30 minutes cumulative. Note the hold time on the pan with a grease pencil.

steps.title: Portion and open the line
steps.instruction: Portion Hungarian Goulash for the Crew onto sheet trays or hotel pans for family-style service. Stack plates, forks, and napkins at the end of the line so late-arriving crew can self-serve without bottlenecking the cook.

steps.title: Serve in bowls
steps.instruction: Taste and adjust salt. Ladle into bowls with sour cream dolloped on top and rye bread on the side. Plan about 5 minutes for this step at crew scale. Keep a backup tray at 200°F for firefighters returning from a call — never serve picked-over pans to late crew. Work in batches if the pan or grill crowding steams food instead of browning — rookies should watch for pale surfaces and adjust heat early.

proTips: A bay leaf in the simmer adds subtle depth—remove before service.
Csipetke noodles are traditional if you want an extra Hungarian touch.
Hot paprika on the side lets crews customize heat without changing the pot.
tonightSpread: Goulash bowls with sour cream, rye bread, and pickled vegetables.
Simple cabbage salad with vinegar dressing.
leftovers: Thicken with a little flour and wrap in pastry for goulash hand pies.
Serve over spaetzle if you have egg noodles gone.
whyCrewsLikeIt: Goulash is cold-weather hall fuel. It is hearty without being greasy, spices are warm not blow-your-head-off, and one pot feeds everyone including the probie who always takes seconds.
mealPrepNotes: Cut beef uniform for even cooking. Stew tastes better the next day. Hold at 165°F in hotel pans with a thin broth layer so meat does not dry.
